articles.author: Konrad
articles.description:
I started building Comparica because I became obsessed with a simple question:
_How do you know what people would actually choose? _
When designing an app, you ask your colleagues, and you say this is better. Are you sure? How do you know your end user will prefer this design over the other? 
We are often so certain. 
After I have done Foundations of User Experience (UX) Design, I am almost certain we do not know.
What I want is to simply ask very fast, compare which option is better! Just give me a vote for one of the many ideas. Just real choices between options.
At first, it looked like a simple polling app, but... it would be also good to know how good I am at such predictions. Am I a total loser, or am I actually the best in that one category (i.e I know what people like to wear, what interior design they choose)?
People genuinely enjoyed comparing almost everything.
Not only products or business ideas, but also:
outfits
memes
profile photos
room designs
random internet debates
everyday decisions
So the project slowly evolved into something closer to a social prediction game.
Users can:
create comparison polls
vote on other people’s choices
predict what the majority will choose
gain points and rankings for accurate predictions
The most interesting part for me so far is discovering how naturally people like comparing things and trying to understand crowd behavior.
The project is still early and evolving, still there is much to do, but it’s finally live:
comparica.com
I’d genuinely love feedback or thoughts on where this kind of social mechanic could evolve 😄
articles.title: I built a platform where people compare things and predict the majority

articles.author: Amphoteric Studio
articles.description:
We recently released a 2D precision platformer on Android, built around a simple question:
What happens if the player doesn't control jumping?
In most platformers, jumping is the core mechanic. It’s reactive and immediate. You press a button, and you jump.
In Crom's Escape, the character jumps automatically.
The player controls only movement, timing, and positioning.
The idea was to shift the challenge away from reaction toward consistency.
Instead of asking:
the game asks:
Removing manual jumping changes how levels are built:
Timing becomes predictable but unforgiving

Movement becomes the primary skill

Small mistakes are amplified



Levels are designed with very low tolerance for error, and failure usually happens quickly.
This is intentional.
Fast retries are part of the core loop.
Early versions felt confusing rather than difficult.
Players tried to jump instinctively.
So the design had to clearly communicate:
The final result is a precision platformer that feels unusual at first but becomes predictable over time.
It’s not designed to be accessible or relaxing — it’s built around repetition and mastery.
Google Play:
https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.amphoteric.cromsescape.game
Trailer:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TixJBd-r9Ck
We’d be curious how you approach gameplay constraints like this.
articles.title: Designing a platformer where you don’t control jumping
